prompt: Bruno has `SELECT` on `sales.orders` but no privilege on the schema `sales`. What happens when he queries the table?
hint: Two grants were needed for one table.

choices.text: It works, because the table grant is the one that counts
choices.why: No. Without USAGE on the schema he cannot look inside it at all.

choices.text: It is refused at the schema
choices.why: Right. USAGE on the schema and SELECT on the table are both required.

choices.text: He sees the column names but no rows
choices.why: No. The statement is refused; there is no partial answer.

choices.text: It works for the owner's rows and no others
choices.why: No. Ownership of rows is not a concept here; the refusal is at the schema.

prompt: Match each letter of `arwdDxt` to the privilege it stands for.
hint: a is append, r is read.

prompt: Ana, without `SET ROLE ipe_owner`, tries to grant `SELECT` on `sales.order_items`. Why is she refused?
hint: What does Ana hold on the data as herself?

choices.text: CREATEROLE forbids granting table privileges to a role she created
choices.why: No. CREATEROLE is about roles; the refusal is about the schema.

choices.text: The table is locked by another session
choices.why: No. A lock would wait, not answer with permission denied.

choices.text: As herself she holds nothing on Ipê's data
choices.why: Right. Her membership in ipe_owner has INHERIT FALSE, so she has to become the owner to grant.

choices.text: Only the superuser grants on tables
choices.why: No. The owner grants, which is what SET ROLE ipe_owner lets her be.

prompt: Ipê hires a second analyst. In the arrangement this lesson builds, what does Ana run?
hint: Privileges belong to the job.

choices.text: GRANT analyst TO the new login
choices.why: Right. One membership, and she has exactly what every analyst has.

choices.text: One GRANT per table the analysts read, to her login
choices.why: No. That is the person-by-person arrangement the lesson replaced.

choices.text: A copy of Bruno's role under her name
choices.why: No. PostgreSQL has no role copy, and the job is what should be shared.

choices.text: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES for her login
choices.why: No. Default privileges are about future objects, not new people.

prompt: In `\drg`, `bruno` is a member of `analyst` with `INHERIT, SET`. What does `INHERIT` give him?
hint: Compare with Ana's membership in ipe_owner.

choices.text: The right to add other people to analyst
choices.why: No. That is ADMIN, which Ana holds.

choices.text: The ownership of every table analysts read
choices.why: No. Membership never transfers ownership.

choices.text: The job's privileges, without having to ask for them
choices.why: Right. With INHERIT the privileges flow to him; with SET alone he would have to SET ROLE analyst.

choices.text: Permission to log in as analyst
choices.why: No. analyst is NOLOGIN; nobody logs in as it.

prompt: Support should be able to close a ticket but never change what a customer wrote. Which grant says that?
hint: A verb can be narrower than a table.

choices.text: GRANT UPDATE ON support.tickets TO support_agent
choices.why: No. That allows updating every column, body included.

choices.text: GRANT UPDATE (status) ON support.tickets TO support_agent
choices.why: Right. The column list makes the decision readable: status and nothing else.

choices.text: GRANT SELECT ON support.tickets TO support_agent WITH GRANT OPTION
choices.why: No. That lets agents pass on reading; it grants no update at all.

choices.text: GRANT TRIGGER ON support.tickets TO support_agent
choices.why: No. TRIGGER lets a role create triggers on the table, which is unrelated.

prompt: Ana runs `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES … GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO analyst` today. Which tables can analysts read because of it?
hint: returns needed its own GRANT.

choices.text: Every table in the schema, old and new
choices.why: No. Existing tables are untouched; that is what GRANT is for.

choices.text: Those the owner creates from now on
choices.why: Right. A default privilege changes the future and never the past.

choices.text: Tables Ana creates as herself
choices.why: No. The rule is for tables ipe_owner creates.

choices.text: None until the server restarts
choices.why: No. deliveries was readable straight away.

prompt: Somebody proposes the same default — `SELECT` for analysts on new tables — for the schema `health`. What is the argument against it?
hint: When is the decision about each future table made?

choices.text: Default privileges do not work on schemas holding health data
choices.why: No. They work on any schema; the question is whether they should.

choices.text: Analysts already read health through the sales grant
choices.why: No. Nobody holds USAGE on health.

choices.text: It would slow down every query on health
choices.why: No. Privileges cost nothing measurable at query time.

choices.text: Each new medical table opens itself
choices.why: Right. Decided once, by somebody thinking of another table: a default is a decision made in advance for tables nobody has designed yet.

prompt: Bruno has `SELECT` on six columns of `sales.customers`. What does `SELECT * FROM sales.customers` return?
hint: The star asks for every column.

choices.text: The six granted columns
choices.why: No. The server refuses the whole statement rather than return a quiet subset.

choices.text: Every column, with the others blanked out
choices.why: No. Nothing is blanked; the statement is refused.

choices.text: permission denied for table customers
choices.why: Right. Naming the granted columns is the way that works.

choices.text: Every column, because SELECT * is exempt
choices.why: No. The star is not exempt from anything.

prompt: From Bruno's count by state, how many of Ipê's customers live in São Paulo?
hint: The first row of the result.

prompt: Analysts cannot select `cpf`, `email`, `full_name` or `birth_date`. Why is the customers data they do see still not anonymous?
hint: Think of a group with one person in it.

choices.text: Their combinations narrow to one person
choices.why: Right. City, sex and sign-up month together narrow a group to one person: column privileges filter what is selected, not what is inferred, and lesson 5 measures it.

choices.text: The hidden columns are still sent and filtered by psql
choices.why: No. The server never sends a column that was not granted.

choices.text: customer_id is the CPF under another name
choices.why: No. It is an internal number, though it does join to other tables.

choices.text: Analysts can read the hidden columns through the catalogue
choices.why: No. The catalogue shows column names, not values.

prompt: Bruno reads `customer_profile`, which reads `birth_date`, and he has no right to `birth_date`. Why does it work?
hint: Whose privileges does the view use?

choices.text: Views ignore privileges entirely
choices.why: No. Privileges are checked, but for the view's owner.

choices.text: A default view reads as its owner
choices.why: Right. ipe_owner can read the whole table, and the view reads it on Bruno's behalf.

choices.text: The age band is stored as a column of its own
choices.why: No. It is computed when the view is read.

choices.text: Bruno inherits birth_date from analyst
choices.why: No. analyst has six columns of customers, and birth_date is not one.

prompt: How many of Ipê's customers does the profile view place in the band `under 18`?
hint: The last row of Bruno's count.

prompt: Which of these make a view a good interface for analysts? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think about precision and stability.

choices.text: It exposes values derived to the precision the question needs
choices.why: Yes. An age band, not a date of birth.

choices.text: It does not grow a column when the table does
choices.why: Yes. A new column reaches analysts only when somebody decides it should.

choices.text: It stops readers filtering down to one person
choices.why: No. A view hides columns; lesson 5 deals with filtering to one person.

choices.text: It makes the query faster than reading the table
choices.why: No. A plain view is expanded into the query; speed is not the point.

prompt: With the region policy in place, how many customers does Carla see?
hint: São Paulo and Rio together.

prompt: Right after row security is enabled on `sales.customers`, Bruno counts 0 customers. Why?
hint: Which roles had a policy at that moment?

choices.text: His column grant was revoked by ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY
choices.why: No. Nothing was revoked; his grants are intact.

choices.text: No policy allowed analysts any row
choices.why: Right. Row security fails closed, and it fails quietly: a valid zero rather than an error.

choices.text: The policy for support agents applies to everybody
choices.why: No. It names support_agent; it does not reach analysts.

choices.text: Analysts are limited to São Paulo and Rio
choices.why: No. Then he would have counted 3,386, not 0.

prompt: After row security is enabled, `site_app` gets `permission denied` on customers, while Bruno got 0 rows. What explains the difference?
hint: Which is checked first, the grant or the policy?

choices.text: site_app connects with a password and Bruno does not
choices.why: No. Both connect with SCRAM passwords.

choices.text: Policies apply to people and not to service accounts
choices.why: No. Policies apply to roles; whether a role is a person does not matter.

choices.text: app_web has no SELECT on the table; analyst does
choices.why: Right. The grant is checked first, and row security narrows a grant, never widens one.

choices.text: The website reads through a view
choices.why: No. Neither of them used a view here.

prompt: A policy written as `USING (___)` lets its roles see every row of the table.
hint: A condition that holds for every row.

prompt: Which of these see every row of `sales.customers` despite its policies, as the lab stands? Choose all that apply.
hint: relforcerowsecurity is f.

choices.text: ipe_owner, the table's owner
choices.why: Yes. The owner is exempt unless the table is in FORCE mode.

choices.text: postgres, the superuser
choices.why: Yes. A superuser and any role with BYPASSRLS skip policies.

choices.text: carla, a support agent
choices.why: No. She is bound by the region policy and sees 3,386.

choices.text: site_app, the website
choices.why: No. It has no SELECT on the table at all.

prompt: Carla saw 6,012 customers through `customer_profile` and 3,386 through the table. What changed when the view was set to `security_invoker = true`?
hint: Whose policies does a view evaluate?

choices.text: The view began to cache only her states
choices.why: No. A view caches nothing.

choices.text: The policy was copied onto the view
choices.why: No. Views do not carry policies of their own.

choices.text: Her membership in support_agent was refreshed
choices.why: No. Her membership never changed.

choices.text: The view checked as her, not its owner
choices.why: Right. Which is also why Bruno was then refused: as himself he lacks birth_date.

prompt: Why is a backup taken by a role with `BYPASSRLS` rather than by an ordinary role?
hint: What would a backup that obeyed the policies contain?

choices.text: Otherwise it holds what its runner sees
choices.why: Right. It has to copy every row, so it runs as a role exempt from policies.

choices.text: BYPASSRLS makes the dump compress better
choices.why: No. Compression has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: Ordinary roles are not allowed to run pg_dump
choices.why: No. Any role can run it; it dumps what that role can read.

choices.text: Policies are disabled at night
choices.why: No. Policies do not depend on the time.

prompt: Why was the first tickets policy, reading `current_setting('ipe.region')`, wrong even though it filtered correctly?
hint: Who chose the value?

choices.text: current_setting is too slow inside a policy
choices.why: No. Speed was never the problem.

choices.text: Carla set the attribute herself
choices.why: Right. An attribute that decides access has to come from somewhere the person cannot write.

choices.text: Custom settings are lost when the session ends
choices.why: No. That is true and irrelevant: she sets it again in the next session.

choices.text: A policy on tickets cannot read the customers table
choices.why: No. The fixed policy reads it.

prompt: With the attribute read from `support.agent_regions`, how many tickets does Carla see, whatever she sets `ipe.region` to?
hint: São Paulo's and Rio's together.

prompt: Match each clause of a policy to what it decides.
hint: One reads, one writes.

pairs.right: which existing rows a role may see, update or delete
which rows a role may write
which roles the policy applies to

right_distractors: which columns a role may select

prompt: In a warehouse, columns are tagged `pii` and people get `region:south` from the identity provider. Who should be able to set each?
hint: The same rule as agent_regions.

choices.text: Each analyst tags the columns they create and declares their own region
choices.why: No. Then the people the rule is about are writing its inputs.

choices.text: Governance of data and of identity, in that order
choices.why: Right. Data governance tags the data, identity governance sets people's attributes, and never the person the rule is about.

choices.text: Whoever runs the query, so the rule fits the task
choices.why: No. That is the session-setting mistake again.

choices.text: The BI tool, from the dashboard's filters
choices.why: No. A dashboard filter is a choice of the viewer.

prompt: The matrix shows `tickets_upd = f` for Carla, though she updated a ticket. Why?
hint: Which question did the function answer?

choices.text: Her update was rolled back
choices.why: No. It returned UPDATE 1 and committed.

choices.text: The matrix ran before the grant
choices.why: No. The grant was made at the start of the lesson.

choices.text: It asks about every column; hers is status
choices.why: Right. has_column_privilege on status would say t.

choices.text: Row security hides her own privileges from her
choices.why: No. Privileges are not rows.

prompt: What makes a matrix like this worth running on a schedule rather than once?
hint: What does a review look for?

choices.text: The functions give different answers at different times of day
choices.why: No. They answer from the grants, which do not depend on the time.

choices.text: Grants expire unless the matrix is run
choices.why: No. Grants do not expire.

choices.text: It refreshes the role memberships
choices.why: No. It reads them; it changes nothing.

choices.text: A change between runs nobody explains
choices.why: Right. A cell that turned t since last month is what a review exists to find.

prompt: Put Lia's offboarding in the order the lesson ran it.
hint: No new sessions first.
items: REASSIGN OWNED BY lia TO ipe_owner

prompt: Why is Lia's role kept with `NOLOGIN` rather than dropped?
hint: Think about the audit trail.

choices.text: So her name in the audit trail still resolves to a role
choices.why: Right. A log line saying lia read a table should point at something that existed.

choices.text: Dropped roles cannot be created again with the same name
choices.why: No. A name can be reused, which is part of the problem with dropping.

choices.text: PostgreSQL refuses to drop a role with an expired password
choices.why: No. Expiry does not prevent dropping.

choices.text: She might come back as an intern next year
choices.why: No. A returning person gets a fresh decision about access.

prompt: Ana created Lia's role, yet `REASSIGN OWNED BY lia` was refused to her. Why?
hint: Administering a role is not becoming it.

choices.text: REASSIGN OWNED only works on roles that can still log in
choices.why: No. It works on NOLOGIN roles; the issue is who runs it.

choices.text: She administers the role, lacking its privileges
choices.why: Right. Only a role with the departing role's privileges may move or drop what it owns.

choices.text: Lia still had an open session
choices.why: No. Open sessions do not block REASSIGN OWNED.

choices.text: ipe_owner refuses objects created by interns
choices.why: No. Ownership transfer has no such rule.

prompt: Bruno read an e-mail address through `sales.customer_email`. Which two facts combined to allow it?
hint: One is about whose privileges the function uses, the other about who may call it.

choices.text: Bruno is an analyst and analysts read e-mail
choices.why: No. analyst has six columns of customers, and email is not one.

choices.text: The search_path setting and a missing index
choices.why: No. The fixed search_path is the part done right.

choices.text: SECURITY DEFINER plus EXECUTE for PUBLIC
choices.why: Right. It ran as ipe_owner, and everybody was allowed to call it.

choices.text: Row security is off for functions
choices.why: No. It is the owner's exemption, not a function rule.

prompt: Match each pattern to what it does.
hint: Each is a grant wider than the decision behind it.

pairs.right: the grantee passes the privilege on
the body runs as the owner

prompt: A new function in PostgreSQL is executable by ___ unless somebody revokes it.
hint: The pseudo-role every role is in.

prompt: Ana enables row security on `support.tickets` with a policy for `support_agent` only. Which reader breaks without an error?
hint: Which role reads tickets and has a grant but no policy?

choices.text: carla, who gets permission denied on every ticket
choices.why: No. She has a policy and sees her states' tickets.

choices.text: site_app, which now gets zero rows back
choices.why: No. app_web has no grant on tickets, so it is refused with an error.

choices.text: ipe_owner, which sees nothing
choices.why: No. The owner is exempt and sees every row.

choices.text: Any role with SELECT and no rule naming it
choices.why: Right. Before enabling, list every role that reads the table and give each a policy.

prompt: Put these checks in the order PostgreSQL applies them to Carla's `SELECT` on customers.
hint: Schema, table, then rows.
items: SELECT on the table, through support_agent
The policy filters the rows by her states
